I also wrote a fuzz tester, `tools/difftest.py`. It generates random queries and checks that all 32 combinations of mode × join × threads × optimize, plus forced worker processes, give the same rows or the same error code. Several thousand queries ran without a mismatch after it found two bugs, both now fixed: a partial result that couldn't be sent back from a worker, and an overflowing constant that vectorized mode evaluated even for NULL rows.

## What I implemented
- **`mode: "row"`**: a row-at-a-time iterator engine, kept as the unoptimized baseline.
- **`mode: "vectorized"`** (also used for `auto`): column batches of 4,096 rows. Expressions run as tight C-level loops (`map`, `compress`, `itemgetter`), with a fast path for batches without NULLs. Operands that could raise an error are only evaluated for rows that need them, matching row mode, so e.g. `b <> 0 AND a/b > 1` never divides by zero. Grouping keeps per-aggregate flat lists instead of one object per group.
- **Joins**: hash, a new sort-merge join (inner and LEFT), and nested loop, all selectable with `join`. Non-equi joins always use nested loops; `auto` picks hash.
- **`threads`**: the planner adds `Gather` nodes that split the driving scan into partitions. Aggregation, top-N and DISTINCT work per partition and are merged in scan order, so results don't depend on the thread count.
- **Optimizer** (all off with `optimize: false`): constant folding, predicate simplification, the existing predicate pushdown and column pruning, greedy join reordering, and top-N for `ORDER BY … LIMIT`.
- **Memory**: the Python garbage collector is paused while queries and loads run, NULL positions are cached per column, and parallel partitions decode only their own row range.

## Main design decisions (documented in README)
- **Parallelism uses forked processes, not threads.** This Python build has the GIL, so threads can't speed up CPU work. Inputs of 200,000+ rows run in forked workers; smaller ones run their partitions one after another in the same thread. That means the `threads: 4` tests on small tables exercise the same partition-and-merge code. A new engine flag, `--parallel-min-rows`, sets the threshold. Timeouts and cancellation kill the workers; I checked this over HTTP and no processes were left behind.
- **Pausing the garbage collector was the single biggest win.** It cut a 1M-row sort from 2.9 s to 0.78 s.
- **Non-selective pipelines aren't parallelized.** At the root or under a full sort, sending every row back from the workers costs more than it saves.

## Measurements (1M rows, medians in ms; machine shared with other jobs, about ±20% noise)

| Query | Phase 4 engine | row | vectorized | vectorized, 4 threads |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GROUP BY, 8 groups (Q2) | 2864 | 446 | 217 | 121 |
| 1M ⋈ 100k join + GROUP BY (Q4) | 1655 | 580 | 241 | 132 |
| Full 1M-row sort (Q8) | 3798 | 985 | 727 | 728 |

The three-way comma join R1 fails on the Phase 4 engine with `RESOURCE_LIMIT`; it now takes 258 ms vectorized. On small tables the optimizer turns it from 7.6 s into 1 ms. Hash joins beat merge joins by 1.1–2×, which is why `auto` picks hash. The README has the full tables.

## Known limitations
- High-cardinality GROUP BY (100k groups) barely speeds up with threads: merging the partial results is serial in the parent.
- Full sorts and queri
